lead: A radio aid is a ground transmitter at a surveyed point, and the receiver on the aircraft turns its signal into one line of position. A point-source aid measures range or bearing to one station: the line is then a circle or a straight line through that station. A hyperbolic aid measures the difference in distance to two stations: the line is a hyperbola. This chapter covers both families — NDB/ADF, VOR, DME, TACAN, LORAN-C and Decca — and how such lines become a fix.
prereq: You need: 5.1 for lines of position, cut angle and the nautical mile.

sections.h3: Point-source aids: bearing or range from one station

blocks.text: A point-source aid has exactly one transmitter, at a surveyed position. The receiver measures one quantity about the line joining aircraft to station. Measure a bearing and the line of position is a straight line through the station. Measure a range and it is a circle centred on the station. One measurement gives one line, so a point-source aid alone cannot fix you.

The automatic direction finder (ADF) works with a non-directional beacon (NDB), a simple transmitter in the low and medium frequency bands, a few hundred kilohertz, radiating equally in all directions. The ADF antenna senses the direction the wavefront arrives from and shows a relative bearing, measured clockwise from the aircraft nose. Adding the heading gives the magnetic bearing to the station — the line of position. Long wavelengths bring trouble: the ionosphere tilts the wavefront after dark (night effect), coastlines refract it, and thunderstorms jam it. NDB bearings are therefore coarse.

The very high frequency omnidirectional range (VOR) transmits at 108–117.95 MHz. The station radiates two 30 Hz signals: a reference whose phase is the same in all directions, and one whose phase rotates with azimuth. The receiver compares the phases and reads a radial — the magnetic bearing of the aircraft measured from the station. Radial 090 means you are east of the station; your track to the station is then 270. A conventional VOR (CVOR) rotates a loop or dipole physically. A Doppler VOR (DVOR) keeps its antennas fixed and switches them round a wide ring, producing the same rotation as a Doppler shift. The wide aperture averages out reflections from buildings and terrain, so DVOR has much smaller site error.

Distance measuring equipment (DME) is two-way ranging at 962–1213 MHz. The aircraft interrogator sends a pulse pair; the ground transponder waits a fixed, known delay of about 50 µs and replies on another frequency. The receiver subtracts the delay and halves the round-trip time to get the slant range r. The ground distance is smaller, because the aircraft sits at height h:

blocks.where: d is the ground range in metres or nautical miles; r is the measured slant range; h is the aircraft height above the transponder, in the same units as d.

blocks.text: The gap matters close in. From 10 km up, an aircraft 100 km out on the ground reads 100.5 km, half a percent long; at 20 km ground distance it reads 22.4 km, twelve percent long. Tactical air navigation (TACAN) is the military version in the 960–1215 MHz band, and one TACAN station gives both bearing and range, so a single transmitter yields a complete fix. Many civil VORs share a site with a DME or TACAN, forming a VORTAC.

sections.h3: The rho-theta fix and the cut angle

blocks.text: Pair a VOR with a co-located DME and one station gives both bearing and range: a rho-theta fix, ρ for range and θ for bearing. The receiver places the aircraft at distance d along radial θ from the surveyed station position. Airliners do this inside the flight management system and draw the result on the navigation display.

Any two-line fix is only as good as its cut angle — the angle at which the lines cross. Lines at 90° fix best; as the cut angle closes, a small measurement error slides the crossing point a long way. Cross-track error from a bearing error Δθ is r × Δθ with Δθ in radians: one degree at 100 nmi is about 1.7 nmi. Dividing the measurement error by sin(cut angle) gives the position error, and the same rule holds for hyperbolic lines.

A hyperbolic aid measures no distance at all. A master and a secondary station transmit pulses at the same instant, synchronised to each other. The receiver times the two arrivals, takes the difference Δt and converts it to a range difference:

blocks.where: Δr is the range difference in metres; c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s is the speed of light; Δt is the measured time difference in seconds.

blocks.text: The aircraft never learns either range, only their difference — and that is enough. The points whose distances to two fixed stations differ by a constant form a hyperbola with the stations at its foci. So one pair of stations gives one hyperbola, one line of position. Take f as the half baseline: a = Δr/2 is the semi-major axis and b = √(f² − a²) is the semi-minor axis. Δr = 0 gives a = 0, and the hyperbola collapses to the straight perpendicular bisector of the baseline. The branch tells the side: the station whose signal arrives first is the nearer one.

A fix needs two hyperbolas, so three stations — one master measured against two secondaries. LORAN-C did this at 100 kHz using ground waves that follow the earth's curve, and its chains covered coastlines and continents to a few hundred metres. Decca compared the phase of continuous low-frequency waves over the North Sea and gave repeated positions to ships and helicopters. Omega, at very low frequency near 10–14 kHz, covered the globe with eight stations and was switched off in the 1990s. Satellite navigation reuses this geometry — see 5.6 — with the receiver's own clock offset carried as one more unknown.

examples.question: A LORAN-C receiver measures a time difference of 100 µs between the master station and one secondary. The master–secondary baseline is 600 km. (a) Find the range difference Δr. (b) Find the semi-major and semi-minor axes of the hyperbola. (c) Which branch is the aircraft on?
steps: The secondary's pulse arrives later, so the aircraft is farther from the secondary. It lies on the branch nearer the master.
examples.answer: Δr = 30.0 km, a = 15.0 km, b = 299.6 km, and the aircraft is on the branch closer to the master station.
examples.check:
c = 3e8
dt = 100e-6
dr = c * dt
a = dr / 2
f = 600e3 / 2
b = (f**2 - a**2) ** 0.5
print(round(dr / 1000, 1))
print(round(a / 1000, 1))
print(round(b / 1000, 1))

examples.question: An aircraft at 9 km altitude reads a DME slant range of 150 km. What is its ground distance from the transponder?

traps: One hyperbola is one line of position, not a fix. Two hyperbolas, hence three stations, are needed; a two-station reading fixes nothing.
DME reads slant range. Directly overhead at 10 km altitude the DME shows 10 km, not zero, and the ground distance is always smaller than the reading.
A VOR radial runs from the station to the aircraft. Radial 090 puts you east of the station and your track to the station is 270; swap the two and the fix is 180° wrong.

A hyperbolic receiver's clock need not be synchronised with the stations — only the stations must agree with each other, because a common clock offset cancels in the difference. In satellite navigation that offset is solved as an extra unknown.
Watch units in Δr = c·Δt: microseconds, not milliseconds. A 100 ms difference would give 30 000 km, larger than the earth.

quiz.q: State the line of position produced by a DME range and by a VOR radial.
quiz.a: DME: a circle centred on the transponder, flown as an arc. VOR radial: a straight line through the station.

quiz.q: Give the frequency bands of VOR and DME.
quiz.a: VOR: 108–117.95 MHz, VHF. DME: 962–1213 MHz, UHF.

quiz.q: Why can a hyperbolic receiver be simpler than a ranging receiver?
quiz.a: It only times the difference between arrivals from stations synchronised to each other. Any offset of its own clock is common to both arrivals and cancels in the difference, so the receiver needs no absolute time reference.

quiz.q: Why does a DVOR have smaller site error than a CVOR?
quiz.a: The DVOR switches antennas round a wide ring, so the bearing information is carried by Doppler shift spread over a large aperture. Reflections from nearby obstacles are averaged over that aperture instead of distorting one narrow rotating pattern.

quiz.q: Two stations 400 km apart give a time difference corresponding to Δr = 40 km. Find a and b.
An aircraft at 12 km altitude reads a DME range of 200 km. Find the ground distance.
Why is a hyperbolic fix poor when the aircraft lies on the extension of the baseline?
quiz.a: There the range difference changes very slowly with position, so the hyperbolas reduce to nearly parallel straight lines. The cut angle is shallow and a small timing error moves the crossing point a long way.

quiz.q: A VOR/DME fix is taken with the aircraft 100 nmi from the station, and the bearing is in error by 2°. Estimate the position error across track.
quiz.a: Δθ = 2° = 0.0349 rad; cross-track error = r × Δθ = 100 × 0.0349 = 3.5 nmi, assuming the DME arc crosses the radial at about 90°.

beyond: Not for the exam. Most LORAN-C chains were switched off during the 2010s, and several countries are now building eLoran as a backup to satellite navigation, because a single low-frequency station is harder to jam than a weak signal from orbit. The same time-difference-of-arrival geometry, solved with more receivers, locates mobile phones and tracks airport surface vehicles by multilateration. In research the mathematics is written as a least-squares hyperbolic position solution. Good things to search next: eLoran, TDOA multilateration, and DVOR site error.
